abstract: This article reframes accusations of 'fake news' not as indicators of misinformation per se, but as strategic rhetorical weapons used to delegitimize political opponents. The authors propose the Strategic Delegitimization and Selective Amplification (SDSA) model, which conceptualizes fake news accusations as a triadic interaction between an accuser, a target, and a media outlet that selectively amplifies accusations according to its editorial leanings. Using a novel dataset of 2778 Italian newspaper articles (2020–2024), the study maps who accuses whom of spreading fake news and how partisan media condition coverage, finding that populist parties are disproportionately targeted rather than being the main accusers, and that media selectivity operates primarily by emphasizing accusations against ideologically distant actors.
key_claims: Fake news accusations function as tools of epistemic delegitimization in negative campaigning, transforming factual disagreement ('you are wrong') into moralized accusations of deception ('you lie'), rather than being simply about the accuracy of content.

The proposed SDSA model integrates three literatures — 'fake news' as a strategic label, negative campaigning, and political parallelism — to explain the production, circulation, and amplification of fake news accusations.
Contrary to common assumption, populist parties are not significantly more likely to be accusers, but are disproportionately positioned as targets of fake news accusations.

Contemporary political parallelism operates less through affirmative amplification of allied voices and more through 'negative epistemic gatekeeping' — marking certain actors (especially populists) as unreliable.
Media selectivity operates primarily on the target/accused dimension rather than the source/accuser dimension.
methods: Constructed a novel corpus of 2778 newspaper articles from five Italian newspapers (La Repubblica, Corriere della Sera, il Giornale, il Fatto Quotidiano, il Manifesto) via the Factiva database, searching for 'fake news' / 'notizia falsa' alongside references to major parties or leaders (2020–2024).
Used GPT-4 with zero-shot prompting to classify actors in extracted text windows as 'accuser' or 'accused' and output structured JSON; party affiliations assigned manually.
Validated LLM coding against a stratified 5% manually annotated sample (stratified by newspaper), achieving 75% agreement; final analytical dataset of 1082 coded observations.
Classified parties as populist/non-populist using The PopuList (Rooduijn et al., 2023) and measured ideological placement using Chapel Hill Expert Survey (CHES) left–right scores.

Analytical techniques: chi-square and proportion tests for role distributions; negative binomial regression modeling accusation counts between party pairs as a function of ideological distance; descriptive party-level share analyses across newspapers to assess selective amplification.
findings: Populist parties accounted for 50.9% of accusations made — not significantly above parity (p=.41), so H1 (populists as more frequent accusers) was not supported.

Populist parties constituted ~70% (69.9%) of accused actors, a statistically significant majority (p<.001), strongly supporting H2; Lega and FdI were especially likely to be accused. Chi-square test showed a significant association between party type and role (χ²(1)=18.58, p<.001), driven by the accused role.

Over 80% of accusation dyads occurred across opposing ideological blocs; negative binomial regression showed each one-point increase in left–right distance associated with ~10% more accusations, but the effect was not statistically significant (p=.11), giving only suggestive support for H3.
H4 (newspapers amplify accusations by ideologically proximate parties) received only weak support; in most outlets proximate parties accounted for less than half of accusers.

H5 (newspapers emphasize accusations against ideologically distant parties) received strong support in four of five newspapers (La Repubblica 84.4%, il Manifesto 77.8%, il Fatto Quotidiano 59.4%, Corriere della Sera 56.2%).

Il Giornale was a deviant case, showing symmetrical distribution (~41% accusers, ~40% accused) despite strong right-wing positioning, suggesting it normalizes fake news rhetoric rather than using it selectively.
contributions: Advances the study of negative campaigning by incorporating media selectivity into the analysis of epistemic delegitimization.
Provides systematic empirical evidence on how fake news discourse functions in a multiparty, high-parallelism system (Italy) via a novel large-scale dataset.
Clarifies the dual role of populist parties as both accusers and (especially) targets, and shows how editorial tendencies structure coverage.
Introduces the SDSA model as a replicable analytical framework applicable across different media systems.
Reconceptualizes contemporary political parallelism as operating through 'negative epistemic gatekeeping' rather than affirmative amplification of allied voices.
framing: The paper positions itself within political communication scholarship on 'fake news' as a strategic discursive label (Egelhofer and Lecheler), negative campaigning, populism, and Hallin and Mancini's theory of political parallelism. It uses the Italian case as a test of how partisan media–politics alignment persists in a 'post-ideological' context marked by the decline of party press and eroding institutional trust, contributing to debates over epistemic legitimacy and affective polarization in mediatized democracies.
